blocks.text: The direction of electron flow in the wires of the external circuit is deduced by comparing the E standard values of the two half-cells. In Figure 10.9 the voltages are Ag+(aq) + e- giving Ag(s), +0.80 V, and Zn2+(aq) + 2e- giving Zn(s), -0.76 V. The relative values show that Zn2+ ions are more difficult to reduce than Ag+ ions, so zinc metal loses electrons to the Ag+/Ag half-cell and Ag+ ions accept electrons from the Zn2+/Zn half-cell. The electrons move through the wires in the external circuit, not through the electrolyte solution: the flow is from the Zn2+/Zn half-cell to the Ag+/Ag half-cell, from the negative pole to the positive pole, since the more positive pole attracts the negative electrons.

blocks.alt: Six half-reactions in order of standard electrode potential: Cl2/Cl- +1.36, Ag+/Ag +0.80, Cu2+/Cu +0.34, H+/H2 0.00, Zn2+/Zn -0.76 and Mg2+/Mg -2.38 V. An arrow up the left shows the oxidising power of the left-hand species increasing, with Cl2 the strongest oxidising agent; an arrow down the right shows the reducing power of the right-hand species increasing, with Mg the strongest reducing agent.

blocks.prompt: In a cell made from Fe2+/Fe (-0.44 V) and Cu2+/Cu (+0.34 V), which way do electrons flow and which way do ions move?
blocks.explanation: Electrons flow through the wire from the iron electrode (more negative, the negative pole, where Fe is oxidised) to the copper electrode (positive pole, where Cu2+ is reduced). In the salt bridge cations drift towards the copper half-cell and anions towards the iron half-cell to keep both solutions neutral; electrons never pass through the solutions.

items: Electrons flow in the external wires from the half-cell with the more negative E standard (negative pole, Zn) to the more positive (positive pole, Ag); never through the electrolyte.
